title: Pharmacy studies at Howard and leaving to pursue the trumpet
summary: He works for a neighborhood apothecary, enters Howard's pharmacy college, then leaves in his third year to commit to trumpet, without family doubts.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: Yes. It looks like, from what I’ve read, you took a bit of a detour when it came time for college that you were pursuing a career in pharmacy?

Yeah well this is a Hollywood story you know. So you know, in my last couple of years of high school, of course I was in the swing band and the marching band and the concert band in high school so I’m with that trumpet all the time. And so I wanted to earn a little money and I asked the neighborhood pharmacist, which I believe probably was the only black-owned apothecary, because that’s what it was, it wasn’t, they didn’t have the words “pharmacy” on their window, it was an apothecary. It was really, I mean if you go into the weeds of pharmacology it’s about the apothecary and so I’m sitting, waiting — my job was to deliver the medicine to the neighborhood folks and I’m sitting watching them, the two doctors. Because they weren’t called pharmacists, they were doctors you know. The title pharmacist was there but you know they were considered pharmacists, I mean apothecarians. So anyway I’m sitting watching them and they are using this mortar and pestle you know and mixing this medicine. And I’m saying to myself, as I was to surmise a little bit later, that if they didn’t mix it right the patient just might die. I mean today, you know, in the modern world although folks are trained in pharmacology and they know what the meds are that go into it, but basically when a prescription comes in they just press a ferris wheel and —

There it is, the bottle is there. At that time the pharmacist, he had to mix most of the medicine. And this just intrigued the hell out of me you know. And I said I want to do that. And it didn’t dawn on me that it would be any separation from dealing with that and music, so I mean I was accepted at the famous Howard University College of Pharmacy and off I went. And in my third year, most of my time was there — although I was in my

pharmacy studies and pharmaceuticals and everything, but a lot of my time was spent in the fine arts building you know, in the music, down in the dungeons of one of those practice rooms. And in my third year I just, you know after working really hard on that trumpet I made a calculated decision that yes I could go on and finish but if I didn’t get this down you know what I was planning to do on the trumpet, so off I went back home and the rest is history you know.

Did your family members or your friends question that decision? And in your head did you consider that making a career as a musician was going to be challenging and probably less of an income than being a pharmacist?

Not for a nanosecond. Because you know the music was in my head since I was five years old. And once I realized that I could actually produce that on the trumpet too, all I wanted to do was belong, nothing more, nothing less. And I didn’t think about the fact that it was very chancy to leave my studies in college and go on this, you know, glorious adventure you know. And I did get lucky though, and it takes luck, a bit of luck in this, to meet the right people or be in the right place at the right time. And that sort of really helped to kick-start me just on full steam ahead, this is my life’s work.
